author: Arezu Fayyazi
title: Afghan Women Are Restricted, But They Cannot Be Silenced. They Continue to Be Agents of Change in Afghanistan.
content:
Afghan women have been living under one of the most repressive systems in the world, as the Taliban continue to impose restrictive edicts – over 160 in total to date. These orders restrict their ability to work, attend school, move freely and even leave their homes without a male guardian. Yet despite the barriers the Taliban have imposed, Afghan women continue to be at the forefront of efforts to build peace and stability in Afghanistan.

Peace and security extends beyond just political conversations. They also include the “daily strategies Afghan women employ to defend human rights and generate conditions for peace.” According to a report by the Georgetown Institute for Women, Peace, and Security, 81% of Afghan women participate in efforts focused on women’s and girl’s education, 64% in economic empowerment, and another 54% in health & reproductive rights and services. Afghan women are also engaged in health and reproductive rights and services, by roughly 9%, compared to women from other regions of South Asia.

These figures demonstrate the perseverance, leadership, and problem solving of Afghan women. Afghanistan is facing a reproductive health crisis, with maternal mortality rapidly increasing since the Taliban took over in 2021. author: Kiara Green
title: 2026 Midterm Elections: A Guide to Voting and Making an Informed Choice
content:
With Election Day less than 40 days away, voters across the country are preparing to cast ballots in the 2026 midterm elections. On November 3, voters will decide congressional, state, and local races, and ballot measures in states across the country.

With so many races and issues on the same ballot, it is crucial that citizens are making informed decisions when they cast their ballot. Voters may encounter campaign advertisements, social media posts, news coverage, and information from candidates themselves, making it difficult to find a clear overview of where candidates stand on the issues.

One resource that can help is guides.vote, a non-partisan voter guide that provides information about candidates and their stances on a range of issues.

Guides.vote produces nonpartisan voter guides with the help of experienced editors, researchers, and veteran journalists. The guides provide information about candidates’ positions on issues and are designed to help voters compare candidates before casting their ballots.

These guides are available digitally and in print and are offered in both English or Spanish. Guides.vote currently includes 2026 election information for races in states across the country.

author: Sofia Little
title: Get the Flock Out
content:
On September 23rd, the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism held a hearing titled “Always Watching: Flock’s Nationwide AI Surveillance Network,” examining the privacy risks, data sharing, and misuse of private automated license plate reader (ALPR) networks.

The hearing was chaired by Sen. Hawley (R-MO) and featured five witnesses, including Lindsey Isaacs, a wrongfully accused driver, Alasdair Whitney from Legislative Counsel Institute for Justice, Sheriff Ross Teeple, Benn Jordan, a self-proclaimed “hacker”, and policy counsel analyst Chad Marlow from the ACLU, where they have coined a campaign called “Get the Flock Out.”

The hearing highlighted pertinent concerns about how ALPR technology can be used and shared. Public concern about Flock cameras has also grown in recent months. A September 2026 Navigator Research survey found that 62% of registered voters were concerned about Flock camera use, including 66% of Democrats, 55% of Republicans, and 70% of Independents.

Flock Safety was founded in 2017 by CEO Garrett Langley, operating as a small startup meant to provide ALPR cameras to homeowners associations and neighborhoods looking to reduce petty theft and local property crimes. author: Bianca Blell
title: Virginia Voters Will Decide the Future of Reproductive Freedom, Marriage Equality, and Voting Rights This November
content:
On November 3rd, Virginia voters will decide on three proposed amendments to the state constitution concerning reproductive freedom, marriage, and voting rights. The amendments would add a constitutional right to reproductive freedom, remove Virginia’s constitutional prohibition on same-sex marriage and require equal treatment of marriages, and automatically restore voting rights to people convicted of felonies upon release of incarceration.

Together, the measures represent one of the most consequential ballot slates for civil rights in the state’s recent history, including a rare opportunity for voters to enshrine protections directly into the state constitution, beyond the reach of a hostile legislature or a change in administration. All three amendments were approved by the General Assembly through Virginia’s constitutional amendment process and will appear on the November 2026 ballot.

The first amendment establishes a constitutional right to reproductive freedom and access. The amendment defines the right as including decisions about prenatal care, childbirth, postpartum care, contraception, abortion care, miscarriage management, and fertility care. It would also prohibit the Commonwealth from penalizing or prosecuting individuals for exercising those rights, as well as doctors, nurses, and others who assist patients with their voluntary consent.

author: FMF Staff
title: Five Years Later, Girls in Afghanistan Are Still Waiting For School Doors To Open
content:
For five years, girls above sixth grade have been barred from classrooms, making Afghanistan the only country in the world where girls are banned from secondary and higher education.

The ban was initially said to be a temporary measure but has now defined half a decade of life for millions of Afghan girls. For them, these years were supposed to be spent in classrooms, preparing for university, building careers, and planning their futures. Instead, they have been spending time waiting.

According to United Nations data, 2.6 million girls have been denied their right to education since the ban began, a policy that experts warn will have long-term consequences not only for girls, but for Afghanistan’s economy, health system, and future development. UNICEF has warned that if the ban continues, millions more girls will be deprived of education by the end of the decade. The ban has already dismantled the pipeline for female doctors and midwives. The maternal and infant mortality rate has already gone up and is only expected to go higher.

When looking beyond the statistics, we see the actual lives that have been put on pause for 5 years.

author: Sofia Little
title: Put the Gun Down: The Intersection between Domestic Violence and Gun Violence
content:
October 1st marks the beginning of Domestic Violence Awareness Month, a month dedicated to bringing attention to domestic violence and supporting efforts to prevent it. Domestic violence can include physical violence, sexual violence, stalking and psychological aggression. These forms of violence affect millions of Americans each year, with perpetrators often being current or former intimate partners. More than one in three U.S. women experience a form of domestic violence in their lifetime.

On September 16, 2026, the Violence Policy Center (VPC) released a report titled, “When Men Murder Women: An Analysis of 2024 Homicide Data.” In 2024, nearly 2,400 women were killed by men, and of these, 86.9% knew their killer—nearly nine out of 10. Firearms were used in 63.4% of these homicides.

Albeit widespread, affecting women across racial and ethnic groups and socioeconomic status, domestic violence disproportionately affects historically marginalized groups. Although Black women only make up 14.1% of the women in the United States, 30.3% of women killed by men in single victim/single offender incidents were Black.

author: Lillian Kollross
title: Ectopic Pregnancy Deaths Have Nearly Doubled: Are Abortion Bans the Cause?
content:
The number of ectopic pregnancy deaths has doubled over the past five years, according to a recent ProPublica analysis of federal data. Almost 200 women have died from ectopic pregnancy between 2020 and 2025. While ectopic pregnancy deaths increased nationwide, the increase was greater in states with strict abortion bans.

An ectopic pregnancy occurs when a fertilized egg implants outside of the uterus, most commonly in the fallopian tubes. The pregnancy cannot develop normally outside of the uterus. If left untreated, the egg will continue to develop until the fallopian tubes rupture, leading to life-threatening internal bleeding.

Ectopic pregnancies are relatively rare, making up about 2% of all pregnancies, they are still the leading cause of death for women in their first trimester. Since hospitals are not required to report ectopic pregnancies, the exact number of cases is difficult to determine.

However, according to maternal health experts, women should not be dying from ectopic pregnancies. “A death related to ectopic pregnancy should really be a never event,” said Dr. Alice Abernathy, a Philadelphia-based OB-GYN.

author: Sara Fayyazi
title: Nepal’s Floods Are Putting Women and Girls at Greater Risk
content:
As devastating floods continue to affect communities across Nepal, women and girls are facing increased risks of hunger, violence, exploitation, and displacement.

On August 26, a devastating flash flood struck Nepal, destroying homes, roads, bridges and critical infrastructure across several regions near the Nepal-Tibet border. More than 500 people have been killed, nearly 1,000 remain unaccounted for, and around 10,000 homes have been destroyed. But as the communities respond to the disaster, women and girls are facing additional challenges.

According to UN Women, 157,050 women and girls in the districts of Rasuwa and Nuwakot have been affected by the floods. The organization has warned that the disaster is increasing existing risks of violence and exploitation while limiting access to health care and other essential services.

Natural disasters do not affect everyone equally and existing inequalities can become more severe when homes, schools, hospitals and other essential services are destroyed. For women and girls who already face barriers to resources, losing access to these services can put their safety and livelihoods at additional risk. Access to food and water is a particular concern. Flooding has damaged infrastructure and disrupted essential services, leaving survivors facing shortages.

author: Lillian Kollross
title: One Louisiana Case Could End Telehealth Abortions for the Whole Country
content:
On September 9, the US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit in New Orleans heard oral arguments in Louisiana v. U.S. Food and Drug Administration, a case that could restrict access to mifepristone nationwide. Louisiana is challenging changes the FDA made to the drug’s Risk Evaluation and Mitigation Strategy (REMS) in 2023, which removed the requirement that mifepristone be dispensed in person and allowed the medication to be prescribed through telehealth and sent by mail. Mifepristone has been FDA-approved since 2000 and is safe and effective.

Louisiana argues that the FDA’s changes were unlawful and interfere with the state’s ability to enforce its abortion restrictions. In January, Louisiana’s Attorney General Liz Murrill testified before a Senate committee that the “Biden administration knowingly and intentionally undermined Dobbs” by allowing mifepristone to be mailed to patients in states with abortion restrictions.

Since the fall of Roe, the number of clinician-provided abortions has almost doubled, largely thanks to telehealth.

The case could have consequences far beyond Louisiana. Louisiana is seeking to reinstate the in-person dispensing requirement nationwide, which would prevent patients from receiving mifepristone through telehealth, mail, or retail pharmacies. author: Bianca Blell
title: Record ICE Arrests Reveal the Expanding Reach of Immigration Enforcement
content:
In June of 2026, US immigration officers, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), arrested a record of 43,138 people. The figure represents the highest number of arrests since President Donald Trump took office in January 2025 and an increase of 5,450 people from early April, an almost 15% difference. The increase comes as immigration enforcement operations have expanded across the country.

This three-month gap in data raises concerns about transparency. Since 2019, Congress has required ICE to publish data on arrests, detentions, and deportations every two weeks. However, the agency did not publish updated figures between early April and July. ICE attributed the delay to a series of government shutdowns.

As of July 11, 65,765 immigrants were detained at detention centers across the country, compared with a record of 70,700 people in January. Since Trump was sworn in this term, over 610,000 immigrants have been detained. The latest figures show that people without a criminal history continue to make up a larger share of those detained than people with pending charges or criminal convictions.

author: Arezu Fayyazi
title: No Girls and women in Classrooms. No Women in Health Clinics. Afghanistan’s Healthcare Crisis Deepens by the Day.
content:
It has been five years since women and girls in Afghanistan have been among the primary targets of the Taliban regime. Their rights to go to school, go to work, and even leave their homes have been taken away. A direct consequence of these restrictions is a crumbling health system, under pressure from a lack of female medical professionals, Taliban restrictions, and funding cuts that threaten to keep health facilities open.

One of the first Taliban orders was to ban women from pursuing higher education and to ban all girls from attending school beyond grade six. According to UNICEF, more than 2.6 million girls do not have access to education as a result of the Taliban’s ban. Other edicts target women’s freedom of movement, including restrictions that prevent women from leaving their homes or going to health clinics without a male family member. These edicts have built on one another to the point where Afghanistan’s education and health systems are being systematically dismantled. The pipeline that once supplied the workforce with trained and skilled professionals is disappearing, creating major long-term consequences for the health system and the country’s workforce.

author: Marcelle Edenlord
title: The Absence of Affordable Child Care is Keeping Women Out of the Workforce
content:
On September 1, the House Education and Workforce Subcommittee on Early Childhood, Elementary, and Secondary Education held a hearing titled “Supporting Working Families: State-Led Child Care Solutions.” The hearing examined how states are addressing the labor and child care crisis and highlighted the growing need for affordable, quality child care and its relation to women in the workforce.

Women have long played a critical role in the US workforce, but in 2025 alone, more than 455,000 women exited. During the same period, the labor-force participation rate for women with bachelor’s degrees fell from 70.3% in September 2024 to 67.7% in July 2025.

Affordable, quality child care is essential for parents who want to remain or enter the workforce. During the hearing, Rep. Bonamici (OR-1) stated, “when parents can’t find quality child care, they reduce their hours, turn down promotions, or leave the workforce entirely.” Limited access to child care can make it more difficult for women to advance their careers, but also detrimental to the economy. The lack of affordable child care costs the US economy an estimated $172 billion annually in lost earnings, productivity, and revenue.
